text.p: New England Electric System's plans to divest its generating capacity are already being questioned by those who helped draft the restructuring agreement with the utility.
NEES would like to find one new owner for the facilities, Chief Financial Officer Alfred Houston told Reuters.
"We'd prefer if you didn't," responded Alan Nogee, a senior energy analyst with the Union of Concerned Scientists, one of the groups involved in the negotiating the settlement.
The company is concerned about the welfare of employees of the generating facilities, Houston explained.
Houston and Agee were panel members at the U.S. Department of Energy's initial town forum on electricity industry restructuring in Sayreville, N.J., last week.

In a competitive industry, NEES said, its retail companies -- Massachusetts Electric Co, Narragansett Electric Co and Granite State Electric Co -- will become "wire companies," continuing to deliver electricity to customers and to provide related services, but no longer purchasing power for customers in most cases.
That "most cases" is because of the agreement's basic service provisions, NEES spokeswoman Karen Berardino said.
This requires the distribution companies to purchase power and be suppliers of last resort, she explained.

New England Power will continue to be responsible for high-voltage transmission of electricity, NEES said, noting its transmission and distribution units will remain regulated by the state and federal governments.
NEES said it intends to be an active competitor in the sale of electricity through A//Energy, a recently announced joint venture with Eastern Enterprises.

Under the settlement, filed with Massachusettes regulatory officials October 1 by Attorney General Scott Harshbarger, NEES' Massachusetts Electric and New England Power have agreed to implement the Attorney General's "Consumers First" plan.
The settlement was reached with the Attorney General, the Massachusetts Division of Energy Resources and numerous other parties, NEES said.
As previously announced, Consumers First opens the utility wires to competitive electricity suppliers in 1998, and generates at least 10 percent savings for customers.

"In return for our commitment to divest our fossil and hydroelectric generating business, we are assured recovery of the investments we made under the old rules," NEES pointed out in its announcement.

Under the agreement, the NEES companies will sell or spin off ownership of their power plants to a non-affiliated entity or entities, in exchange for the ability to recover sunk costs during the transition to a competitive electricity market.
The market value of the utility's generation fleet, as determined by the divestiture, will be deducted from the amount of stranded investment that the company can recover.

This divestiture must occur by six months after the start of retail competition -- proposed for January 1, 1998 -- or six months after the receipt of all necessary government approvals, whichever is later. The company must file a detailed divestiture plan with state and federal regulators by July 1, 1997. Full divestiture is expected by 1998, it said.

The NEES subsidiaries' generating business consists of nearly 4,000 megawatts of capacity in five states, along with a wholesale energy marketing division. Facilities include fossil-fuel fired plants in Somerset, Salem, Gloucester and Newburyport, Mass.; and in Providence, R.I.
As part of the plan, NEES also will divest its regulated oil and gas business, and potentially its minority interests in five operating nuclear plants in four New England states.
The Consumers First plan is subject to approvals from the state and the federal regulators.

"We expect that the Legislature will review the Consumers First plan and take up legislation in a number of areas, including energy facility siting reform and protection for municipalities that host electric facilities," NEEs said.
